title: How to Create a School of Givers Not Takers
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Drawing on Adam Grant's Giver/Taker/Matcher framework, Dominic Salles argues that school culture is shaped more decisively by who is hired than by any programme or initiative. A single Taker — someone who extracts value from colleagues rather than contributing it — can depress team output by 30–40%, a cost that dwarfs even the uplift from a top-performing Giver. Salles warns that the most dangerous hire is not the obvious Taker but the Agreeable Taker: the colleague who appears warm and collegial while quietly hoarding credit and offloading burden. Matchers, who balance giving and taking, tend to mirror the dominant norm — so in a Taker culture they become Takers too, and in a Giver culture they become Givers. The practical implication is that leaders must screen hard for Taker behaviour at the recruitment stage, because cultural remediation after the fact is costly and often fails. Salles closes by noting that the goal is not saintliness but a baseline of generosity that becomes self-sustaining once established.
points: A single Taker on a team reduces collective output by 30–40%, a larger effect than the performance gain from one top Giver — making destructive hires the highest-leverage talent risk a school faces.
The Agreeable Taker is the most dangerous archetype: superficially pleasant and cooperative, this person extracts credit and shifts blame in ways that are hard to detect until the damage is done.
Matchers — the majority of any staff — mirror the prevailing norm. This means one or two Takers can corrupt a whole department's culture, while removing them can flip the dynamic toward generosity.
Recruitment is the highest-leverage point. Screening for Taker behaviour before hiring is far less costly than attempting cultural remediation after a Taker is embedded.
Giver cultures are self-reinforcing: once generosity becomes the visible norm, Matchers adopt it, which further signals to potential Givers that this is a safe place to contribute — a virtuous cycle.
quotes: The cost of a single Taker on a team — that 30–40% drop in collective performance — dwarfs whatever you gain from hiring a superstar Giver.
The Agreeable Taker is the most dangerous hire you will ever make. They seem warm, they seem collaborative, and they are quietly extracting value from everyone around them.
Matchers follow the rewarded norm. Put a Taker in a Giver culture and you corrupt it. Remove the Taker and the Matchers flip back. Culture is more fragile and more recoverable than we think.
The aim is not to hire saints. It is to hire people who default to generosity — and then protect that default by removing those who exploit it.
